about: Source-data errata for the frozen snapshot data/raw/data.js, which stays byte-for-byte as fetched (see data/raw/PROVENANCE.md). scripts/build-graph.ts applies every entry in `text` after it parses the raw file and before it sanitizes or indexes any field. Each `raw` string must occur exactly once in the named field, or the build fails, so a refreshed snapshot cannot silently skip or double-apply a fix. An entry may only move the text toward the published standard or repair markup. It never rewords a standard. `glossaryTables` maps a glossary anchor id that points at a CCSS Glossary table (an id like "[3]") to the definition the popover shows. A bracketed id with no entry here fails the build.

text.why: The snapshot lost the superscript on 1/12, so the example read (1.151/12)^(12t). In the published standard 1/12 is the exponent of 1.15 and 12t is the outer exponent.
text.source: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/HSA/SSE/ (live page sits behind a bot challenge; read via https://web.archive.org/web/20250616161847/https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/HSA/SSE/)
text.citation: CCSS.Math.Content.HSA.SSE.B.3.c: Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions. For example the expression 1.15t can be rewritten as (1.151/12)12t ≈ 1.01212t to reveal the approximate equivalent monthly interest rate if the annual rate is 15%.

text.why:
A mistyped closing tag, escaped as text, so readers saw a literal <\p> at the end of a solution step in the worked example 'Making a ten'. The real

follows it. The standard text itself (desc) is clean. Illustrative Mathematics' own task page carries the same typo, so this is a markup repair, not a wording change.
text.citation:
CCSS.Math.Content.1.OA.C.6: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13). || IM task 1169 solution, as published: "so it is also a 10.\n<\p>\n

"

[3].def: The rules that hold for all numbers: the associative, commutative, and distributive properties, and the identity and inverse properties of addition and multiplication. From the CCSS Glossary, Table 3.
[3].author: Designer-authored definition (2026-09). The source anchor id "[3]" is a pointer to CCSS Glossary Table 3, not a definition.
[3].citation: Mathematics Glossary » Table 3: The properties of operations. Here a, b and c stand for arbitrary numbers in a given number system.
